When you exercise, you trade off temporary damage to your body for further development. This includes damage to your connective tissue, muscle, and bone. It may come as a suprise to you that exercise damages your bones, but it’s just as important or more important than muscle damage, especially if you are lifting weights.

The order I listen the tissues affected by exercising is very important to keep in mind. Connective tissue can be developed very quickly (a few weeks of stretching before practice), and thus can be recovered very quickly from stress/damage (such as pulling a tendon). Muscle takes much longer to develope, and takes much longer to recover after stress/damage. Bone, of course, is the least volatile, and may take a lifetime to hone, and, if broken, are devastating to an athelete.

Because of all this, we can’t put too much stress on the human skeleton. It may be possible to put too much stress on human muscles, but it is very unlikely, as the nerves will be flooded with pain. The skeleton, however, does not send pain when under extreme pressure(unless it breaks of course). Because the skeleton is harder to repair yet less of a complainer when you over burden it, it is crucial that you put as much burden as possible on the muscle, and, by extention, the connective tissue. This is called maintaining form. You may be tempted over a career of lifting to break form if you are impatient with the results of the past month or simply forget over time, but there are drastic consequences.

This applies to all exercise, including running and pushups.

I do wall pushups a bit like that and I keep my wrists straight, fanning out my fingers and pressing on the last joint of each finger, so as to not put pressure on the bone. My palm doesn’t touch the ground, thus pressuring my muscles instead and protecting me if I fall or a heretic pushes me.
